canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Related Rate From an Implicitly Defined Curve
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following ellipse: 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{y^2}{4}=1
$$

 

Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$ and that $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}=\sqrt{2}$ on the curve at the point $(1,\sqrt2),$ find the value of $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}$ at that point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (x)+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{y}{2}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}=\sqrt{2},$ $x=1,$ and $y=\sqrt2,$ and solve $\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}.$  We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (1)+\sqrt{2}\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+1 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Using an Implicitly Defined Curve to Determine a Second Coordinate
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the curve $x^3-\ln y=1.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and that $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}=2$ on the curve at the point where $x=1,$ find the value of $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}$ at that point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}-\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 3{x}^{2}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}=2$ and $x=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}6-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=1$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =1 \\ 1-\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =0 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $y=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{1} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Using the Equation of a Conic Section to Determine a Second Coordinate
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the section of the hyperbola 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{3}-\dfrac{y^2}{2}=1
$$

that lies in the first quadrant. Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$ and that $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}=-2$ on the hyperbola at the point where $x=3,$ find the value of $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}$ at this point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2x}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}=-2$ and $x=3.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2\cdot 3}{3})-(-2)\cdot y & =0 \\ 2\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2y & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-y.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We also want to substitute for $y$, but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=3$ into the equation of the hyperbola.   

At the point where $x=3,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{3}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =2 \\ {y}^{2} & =4 \\ y & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $y > 0$ since we're only interested in the first quadrant. 

Finally, substituting $y= 2,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-y \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Distributions of Squared Random Variables: Many-to-One Transformations
canonical_examples.problem:
The random variable $X$ has the following probability distribution.

| $x$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f_X(x)$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ | $0.3$ | $0.1$ |

Let $Y=1-X^2.$ The distribution of $Y$ is given below.

| $y$ | $a$ | $b$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f_Y(y)$ | $0.3$ | $c$ | $d$ |

Find the values of $a,b,c,$ and $d.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's add a $Y = 1-X^2$ row to our table.

| $x$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | $-3$ | $0$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-3$ |
| $f_X(x)$ | ${\color{red}{0.2}}$ | ${\color{blue}{0.1}}$ | $0.3$ | ${\color{blue}{0.3}}$ | ${\color{red}{0.1}}$ |

From the table, we see that $Y \in \{-3,0,1\}.$ Notice that we now have two columns for both $Y=-3$ and $Y=0.$

We calculate the probabilities associated with each value of $Y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y=-3) & =0.2+0.1 \\ P(Y=0) & =0.1+0.3 \\ P(Y=1) & =0.3\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the following table:

| $y$ | $-3$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f_Y(y)$ | $0.3$ | $0.4$ | $0.3$ |

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Probability Involving a Squared Random Variable
canonical_examples.problem:

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ |

Calculate $P(X^2 = 4).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's first add an $X^2$ row to our table.

| $x^2$ | $16$ | $4$ | $0$ | $4$ | $16$ |

From the second and third rows of our table, we can immediately conclude that 

$$

$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Scalar Function
canonical_examples.problem:
For the transformation $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R,$ defined as

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094602/assets/d8be5d5bd5fa2cd8b618087109678a4f891b08f3788d4946d07bc1b5e4b39a3a.png)

calculate $\boldsymbol f'$ at ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094602/assets/a2dbcf34ea50e451efc96ad2f9a7422a7ae507ca8f74088569110abb25293954.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Suppose a transformation $\boldsymbol{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is defined by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094602/assets/17588b058b1e1fe934e06679836234f0ef35fe4484a558fcc3ec3b2aafbd2620.png) 

where $f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_m$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $\boldsymbol f$ is differentiable at $\mathbf{x},$ then the total derivative of $\boldsymbol f$ at $\mathbf{x},$ denoted $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}),$ is given by the $m \times n$ matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094602/assets/613ba027e9564812a8e050efd69fd98fff3f614f7d2ec69eeb787c628ccabd12.png)

In our case, we have the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094602/assets/87579b882ca6d8c92d4a7adfed575873fd07c36ab20251722c2cc8fc0f0328e8.png)

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y)=2xy, & \,\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y)={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Resultant Force Acting on a Particle Given Its Velocity Vector
canonical_examples.problem:
The velocity $\mathbf v,$ in meters per second, of a particle $P$ of mass $5\,\textrm{kg}$ is given by

$$
\mathbf v =  \langle 3e^{t},\: t^3-t^2\rangle,
$$

where $t\gt 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force acting on the particle when $t=2\,\textrm s.$ Round your final answer to the nearest Newton.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
\mathbf F = m \mathbf a,
$$

 
where $\mathbf F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $\mathbf a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{e}^{t},\,3{t}^{2}-2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $\mathbf F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =5\cdot ⟨3{e}^{t},\,3{t}^{2}-2t⟩ \\  & =⟨15{e}^{t},\,15{t}^{2}-10t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t = 2\,\textrm s,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(2) & =⟨15{e}^{2},\,15({2}^{2})-10(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨15{e}^{2},\,40⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of $\mathbf F(2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|F(2)| & =\sqrt{{(15{e}^{2})}^{2}+{(40)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{225{e}^{4}+1\,600} \\  & ≈118\,\text{N}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest Newton.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Resultant Force Acting on a Particle Given Its Displacement Vector
canonical_examples.problem:
The displacement $\mathbf r,$ in meters, of a particle $P$ of mass $3\,\textrm{kg}$ is given by

$$
\mathbf r =  \langle 3\cos{t}-\sin{t},\: 2\cos{t}\rangle,
$$

where $t\gt 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the resultant force acting on the particle when $t=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\,\textrm s.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
\mathbf F = m \mathbf a,
$$

 
where $\mathbf F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $\mathbf a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we first differentiate $\mathbf r$ to get the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate the velocity vector to get the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $\mathbf F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =3\cdot ⟨-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-9\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-6\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $t = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\,\textrm s,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{3\pi }{4}) & =⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})-9\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}),\,-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{2},\,\frac{6\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨6\sqrt{2},\,3\sqrt{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the resultant force acting on $P$ when $t=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\,\textrm s$ equals $\left\langle 6\sqrt{2},\: 3\sqrt{2}\right\rangle\,\textrm N.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Working With Resultant Forces
canonical_examples.problem:
A particle $P$ of mass $6\,\textrm{kg}$ is subject to the external forces $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2,$ given by

$$
\mathbf F_1 = \left\langle \dfrac2{t+1}+12t,\: \dfrac3{\sqrt t} \right\rangle, \qquad  \mathbf F_2 = \left\langle \dfrac 4{t+1},\: 6\right\rangle,
$$

 
where $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2$ are measured in Newtons and $t > 0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the velocity of $P$ equals $\langle -\ln 3,\:-2\rangle\,\textrm{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\textrm s,$ calculate the speed of $P$ when $t=2\,\textrm s.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Newton's second law states that

$$
\mathbf F = m \mathbf a,
$$

 
where $\mathbf F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $\mathbf a$ is the acceleration.

The resultant force $\mathbf F$ acting on $P$ equals the sum of the forces acting on $P.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F & ={F}_{1}+{F}_{2} \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{t+1}+12t,\,\frac{3}{\sqrt{t}}⟩+⟨\frac{4}{t+1},\,6⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{6}{t+1}+12t,\,\frac{3}{\sqrt{t}}+6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's second law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{F}{m} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot ⟨\frac{6}{t+1}+12t,\,\frac{3}{\sqrt{t}}+6⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t+1}+2t,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the velocity vector $\mathbf v,$ we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\int a\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{t+1}+2t,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (\frac{1}{t+1}+2t)\,\text{d}t,\,\int (\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{t}^{2},\,\sqrt{t}+t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $\mathbf C$ is a (vector) constant of integration. 

We can solve for $\mathbf C$ by substituting $\mathbf v = \langle -\ln 3,\:-2\rangle\,\textrm{m/s}$ and $t=0\,\textrm s$ into the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,-2⟩ & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)+{0}^{2},\,\sqrt{0}+0⟩+C \\ ⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,-2⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩+C \\ C & =⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{t}^{2},\,\sqrt{t}+t⟩+⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{t}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,\sqrt{t}+t-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=2,$ the velocity equals

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+1)+{2}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,\sqrt{2}+2-2⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,\sqrt{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the speed of $P$ when $t=2$ equals the magnitude of $\mathbf v(2).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(2)| & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+2} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Second Moment of a Random Variable
canonical_examples.problem:
A random variable $X$ has the probability distribution given below.

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $0.2$ | $0.25$ | $0.15$ | $0.35$ | $0.05$ |

Calculate $\textrm E[X^2].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $X$ is a discrete random variable with probability mass function $f(x)$ and sample space $S,$ the expected value of $X^2$ is given by

$$
\textrm E[X^2] = \sum\limits_{x \in S} x^2 \cdot f(x).
$$

Summing up the products of each squared value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.2+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.25+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.15+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.35+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.05 \\  & =0\cdot 0.2+1\cdot 0.25+4\cdot 0.15+9\cdot 0.35+16\cdot 0.05 \\  & =4.8.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Higher Moments of a Random Variable
canonical_examples.problem:
A random variable $X$ has the probability distribution given below.

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $0.15$ | $0.25$ | $0.5$ | $0.1$ |

Calculate $\textrm E[X^3].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $X$ is a discrete random variable with probability mass function $f(x)$ and sample space $S,$ the expected value of $X^3$ is given by

$$
\textrm E[X^3] = \sum\limits_{x \in S} x^3 \cdot f(x).
$$

Summing up the products of each cubed value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{3}\cdot f(x) \\  & ={1}^{3}\cdot 0.15+{2}^{3}\cdot 0.25+{3}^{3}\cdot 0.5+{4}^{3}\cdot 0.1 \\  & =1\cdot 0.15+8\cdot 0.25+27\cdot 0.5+64\cdot 0.1 \\  & =0.15+2+13.5+6.4 \\  & =22.05.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Simplifying Expressions Using the Properties of Expected Value
canonical_examples.problem: Compute $\textrm E[X(X-3) + 4]$ if $\textrm E[X^2] = 4$ and $\textrm E[X] = 1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Expanding out the product inside the expected value, using the properties of the expected value, and substituting in the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X(X-3)+4] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}-3X+4] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-3\text{E}[X]+\text{E}[4] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-3\text{E}[X]+4 \\  & =4-3(1)+4 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given the system of differential equations, determine whether the system is almost linear at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x}^\ast= [0, \: 0]^T.$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-{y}^{2}(t)+1-{e}^{x(t)} \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-{x}^{2}(t)+1-{e}^{y(t)}\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
\mathbf{x}' = \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/58d027aeb94fddf42231a86a73de4be306fa6ea22ea7767dbe8a461e91a6f446.png) and 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/bb9297479f2149dfca76e02fb9e314205063fd3a3f967d70eee24235970206b1.png)

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/6ea02cc0d71b67f061adb67ee344cc5474b71e1e34db122b942d2e0ed1531ae8.png)

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{y}^{2}+1-{e}^{x})=-{e}^{x},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{y}^{2}+1-{e}^{x})=-2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{2}+1-{e}^{y})=-2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{x}^{2}+1-{e}^{y})=-{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/8f1e68dd09715b24f0de6c79fdf07af6e9810741e1a6065637db5301cd86ebe0.png)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/ef4a060144a80ac9ecb94a71c407d1537283ecc217ac26ab053e9b8d2fad73e9.png) to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}-{e}^{0} & -2(0) \\ -2(0) & -{e}^{0}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)(-1)-(0)(0) \\  & =1 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{almost linear}}$ at $\mathbf{x}^\ast.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Limit of a Vector Function
canonical_examples.problem:
Calculate  $\lim\limits_{t \to 0} \mathbf{f}(t),$ given that 

$$
\mathbf f (t) = \dfrac{1- e^{t}}{\sin t} \ \mathbf {i}+ \dfrac{\sin t}{t+t^2} \ \mathbf {j} + \dfrac{ e^{t} - e^{-t}}{\sin t} \ \mathbf {k}.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the limit of our vector function, we compute the limit of each component individually:

$$
\lim_{t \to 0}\mathbf f(t) = \left(\lim_{t \to 0} \dfrac{1-e^t}{\sin t}\right)\,\mathbf i + \left( \lim_{t \to 0} \dfrac{\sin t}{t+t^2}\right)\,\mathbf j + \left( \lim_{t \to 0} \dfrac{e^t-e^{-t}}{\sin t} \right)\,\mathbf k
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- The first component can be found using L'Hopital's Rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{1-{e}^{t}}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} & ={lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{(1-{e}^{t})}^{′}}{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{-{e}^{t}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{-{e}^{0}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡0} \\  & =-\frac{1}{1} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

- The second component can be found using a special limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{t+{t}^{2}} & ={lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{t(t+1)} \\  & =({lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{t+1})\cdot ({lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{t}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{0+1})\cdot 1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- The third component can be found using L'Hopital's Rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{e}^{t}-{e}^{-t}}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} & ={lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{({e}^{t}-{e}^{-t})}^{′}}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{t\to 0}\frac{{e}^{t}+{e}^{-t}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{0}+{e}^{-0}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡0} \\  & =\frac{1+1}{1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\lim\limits_{t \to 0}\mathbf f(t) = -\mathbf i + \mathbf j +2\,\mathbf k.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Limit of the Magnitude of a Vector Function
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\lim\limits_{t \to \infty} \| \mathbf f(t) \|$ if $\mathbf f(t)  = \left\langle t^{-1}, \: \left(1+\dfrac{3}{t}\right)^t, \: \dfrac{t^2}{1-t^2} \right\rangle.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the limit of our vector function, we compute the limit of each component individually:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }f(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to \infty }{t}^{-1},\,{lim}_{t\to \infty }{(1+\frac{3}{t})}^{t},\,{lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{{t}^{2}}{1-{t}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }{t}^{-1} & ={lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{t}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

- The second component can be found using a special limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }{(1+\frac{3}{t})}^{t} & ={lim}_{t\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{t/3})}^{t/3}]}^{3} \\  & ={[{lim}_{t\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{t/3})}^{t/3}]}^{3} \\  & =[\,e\,]^{3} \\  & ={e}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{{t}^{2}}{1-{t}^{2}} & ={lim}_{t\to \infty }\frac{1}{\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}-1}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\lim\limits_{t \to \infty}\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle 0, \: e^3, \: -1\right\rangle.
$$

Finally, the limit of $\left\| \mathbf f(t) \right\|$ as $t$ approaches $\infty$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }‖f(t)‖ & =‖{lim}_{t\to \infty }f(t)‖ \\  & =‖⟨0,\,{e}^{3},\,-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+({e}^{3})^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{6}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Limit of a Sum of Vector Functions
canonical_examples.problem:
Find $\displaystyle \lim_{t \to 0} \big[ \mathbf f(t) - 2 \mathbf g(t) \big]$ given that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{t} \\ t\end{aligned}],\,g(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 1 \\ 2t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}{e}^{t} \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\ {e}^{0} \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}g(t)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}1 \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}2t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\ 1 \\ 2(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)-2g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)-2{lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Limit of a Product of Vector Functions
canonical_examples.problem:
Find $\displaystyle \lim_{t \to 2} \left[\mathbf f(t) \cdot \mathbf g(t)\right]$ given that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are defined as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+t\,j+{t}^{2}\,k \\ g(t) & =(2-t)\,i+\frac{6}{t}\,j-4\,k\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}f(t) & =({lim}_{t\to 2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\,i+({lim}_{t\to 2}t)\,j+({lim}_{t\to 2}{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\,i+2\,j+{2}^{2}\,k \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,i+2\,j+4\,k, \\ {lim}_{t\to 2}g(t) & =({lim}_{t\to 2}(2-t))\,i+({lim}_{t\to 2}\frac{6}{t})\,j+({lim}_{t\to 2}(-4))\,k \\  & =(2-2)\,i+\frac{6}{2}\,j+(-4)\,k \\  & =0\,i+3\,j-4\,k \\  & =3\,j-4\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2}[f(t)\cdot g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 2}f(t)\cdot {lim}_{t\to 2}g(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,i+2\,j+4\,k)\cdot (3\,j-4\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot 0+2\cdot 3+4\cdot (-4) \\  & =-10\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Singular Values of a Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- Any $1\times4$ matrix $A$ has at most $1$ singular value.

- Any $4\times2$ matrix $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- The matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14078642/assets/a33b8a531dc91b49f01826cd7fcedaae2ee3144b5205bbe724efa9f29a302b37.png) has one negative singular value.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $1 \times 4$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $4\times 1$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $4 \times 4$ matrix: 

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times {\large 1}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 1} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A} =  
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. Since $A$ is a $4 \times 2$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $2\times 4$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix: 

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 4}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ cannot have a negative singular value.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Singular Values of a Square Matrix
canonical_examples.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14078642/assets/9a78a1681842653fabade3354cc5e885f0bfc32eefa3b56e9d1faf716dc5d97b.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$  

First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )^{2}-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Singular Values of a Rectangular Matrix
canonical_examples.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14078642/assets/5d2eb1db497eeb2f3e24feaa1ac70547a48cc55d1eeea22da91231b1d1275df8.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$  

First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1-\lambda  \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )^{2}-(1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda ) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing Variance Using the Definition Given a Probability Mass Function
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $X$ be the number obtained by a spinner with four sections labeled $1, 2, 3, 4.$ The probability mass function $f(x)$ of $X$ is shown in the table below. What is $\textrm{Var}[X]?$

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{4}$ | $\dfrac{1}{3}$ | $\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The variance of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \sum\limits_{x \in S} (x - \textrm E[X])^2 \cdot f(x).
$$

First, we need to compute $\textrm E[X].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3)+4\cdot f(4) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{6})+2(\frac{1}{4})+3(\frac{1}{3})+4(\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\textrm E[X]=\dfrac{8}{3}$ into the variance formula, we get

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \sum\limits_{x \in S} \left(x - \dfrac{8}{3} \right)^2 \cdot f(x).
$$

Now, we compute the variance as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & ={(1-\frac{8}{3})}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{(2-\frac{8}{3})}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{(3-\frac{8}{3})}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{(4-\frac{8}{3})}^{2}\cdot f(4) \\  & =\frac{25}{9}\cdot f(1)+\frac{4}{9}\cdot f(2)+\frac{1}{9}\cdot f(3)+\frac{16}{9}\cdot f(4) \\  & =\frac{25}{9}(\frac{1}{6})+\frac{4}{9}\cdot (\frac{1}{4})+\frac{1}{9}\cdot (\frac{1}{3})+\frac{16}{9}(\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{19}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing Variance Given the Expected Value of a Random Variable and Its Square
canonical_examples.problem: If $\textrm E[X] = 4$ and $\textrm E[X^2] = 21,$ then what is $\textrm{Var}[X]?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can compute the variance of a discrete random variable $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm E[X^2] - \textrm E[X]^2
$$

Substituting the given values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =21-{4}^{2} \\  & =21-16 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing Variance Given a Probability Mass Function
canonical_examples.problem: A fair die with sides labeled with numbers $1$ through $6$ is thrown once. If $X$ is the outcome of the die, what is the variance of $X?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can compute the variance of a discrete random variable $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm E[X^2] - \textrm E[X]^2
$$

First, we need to compute the probability mass function $f(x).$ Here, there are $6$ possible outcomes ($1,2,3,4,5,6$) and each outcome has the same probability, so the probability mass function is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ |

Next, we compute $\textrm E[X].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3)+4\cdot f(4)+5\cdot f(5)+6\cdot f(6) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{6})+2(\frac{1}{6})+3(\frac{1}{6})+4(\frac{1}{6})+5(\frac{1}{6})+6(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =\frac{7}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $\textrm E[X^2].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X^2$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{4}^{2}\cdot f(4)+{5}^{2}\cdot f(5)+{6}^{2}\cdot f(6) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{6})+4(\frac{1}{6})+9(\frac{1}{6})+16(\frac{1}{6})+25(\frac{1}{6})+36(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =\frac{91}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{91}{6}-{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{91}{6}-\frac{49}{4} \\  & =\frac{35}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Standard Deviation of a Random Variable
canonical_examples.problem: A fair die with sides labeled with numbers $1$ through $6$ is thrown once. If $X$ is the outcome of the die, what is $\textrm{SD}[X]?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is defined as

$$
\textrm{SD}[X] = \sqrt{ \textrm{Var}[X] },
$$

where the variance can be computed using the following formula:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm E[X^2] - \textrm E[X]^2
$$

First, we need to compute the probability mass function $f(x).$ Here, there are $6$ possible outcomes ($1,2,3,4,5,6$) and each outcome has the same probability, so the probability mass function is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ | $\dfrac{1}{6}$ |

Next, we compute $\textrm E[X].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3)+4\cdot f(4)+5\cdot f(5)+6\cdot f(6) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{6})+2(\frac{1}{6})+3(\frac{1}{6})+4(\frac{1}{6})+5(\frac{1}{6})+6(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =\frac{7}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $\textrm E[X^2].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X^2$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{4}^{2}\cdot f(4)+{5}^{2}\cdot f(5)+{6}^{2}\cdot f(6) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{6})+4(\frac{1}{6})+9(\frac{1}{6})+16(\frac{1}{6})+25(\frac{1}{6})+36(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =\frac{91}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{91}{6}-{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{91}{6}-\frac{49}{4} \\  & =\frac{35}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{35}{12}}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying and Interpreting the Lotka-Volterra Model
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=-8x+2xy \\ {y}^{′}=4y-xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above for the functions $x(t)$ and $y(t).$ Provide an interpretation of each equation in the model.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model is given by

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d$ are positive real constants. 

First, recall that a derivative represents a rate of change.

For the $x'$ equation, we have

$$
x' = -8x + 2xy.
$$

Therefore, $x$ must represent the predator. Indeed,

- it decays exponentially in the absence of prey (the $-8x$ term), and

- increases when interacting with prey (the $2xy$ term).

For the $y'$ equation, we have

$$
y' = 4y - xy.
$$

Therefore, $y$ must represent the prey. Indeed, 

- it grows exponentially in the absence of predators (the $4y$ term), and

- decreases when interacting with predators (the $-xy$ term).

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Equilibrium Points of the Lotka-Volterra System
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=-4x+7xy \\ {y}^{′}=9y-5xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey. Find the nonzero equilibrium of the model.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-4x+7xy=0 \\ 9y-5xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-4x+7xy & =0 \\ x(-4+7y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\dfrac{4}{7}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}9y-5(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\dfrac{4}{7},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}9y-5xy & =0 \\ y(9-5x) & =0 \\ \frac{4}{7}(9-5x) & =0 \\ 9-5x & =0 \\ x & =\frac{9}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $\left(\dfrac{9}{5}, \dfrac{4}{7}\right).$

Therefore, the nonzero equilibrium of the model is
$\left( \dfrac{9}{5}, \dfrac{4}{7} \right).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Classifying Equilibria of the Lotka-Volterra Model
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=-0.4x+0.4xy \\ {y}^{′}=y-4xy\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[0.25, \, 1]^T,$ and classify this equilibrium point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=-0.4x+0.4xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=y-4xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.4x+0.4xy)=-0.4+0.4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.4x+0.4xy)=0.4x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-4xy)=-4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-4xy)=1-4x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094872/assets/e526dd9bda292c2a25920b8248820f3ed88c0bc4c4a55e3ba3f2db925af486d8.png)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094872/assets/cc6e0f2742f419fc8f2c09bf69c97f72d7e7f1ca0d98c3845996e216849f4316.png) to get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094872/assets/bcc787d9cceae4a7280c6af84c0d7bf95c15dfc90cf9e3bdedf2a52362c1b225.png)

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & 0.1 \\ -4 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-(-4)\cdot 0.1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues $\lambda_{1,2} = \pm 0.2\sqrt{10}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is a stable center.

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source).

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Continuity of a Vector Function
canonical_examples.problem: Is the vector function $\mathbf f(t) = -\sin t \,\mathbf i + (t^2 + 1)\,\mathbf j + \tan t\,\mathbf k$ continuous at $t = 0?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's compute the limit of $\mathbf f (t)$ as $t$ approaches $0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t) & =⟨{lim}_{t\to 0}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,{lim}_{t\to 0}({t}^{2}+1),\,{lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,{0}^{2}+1,\,\operatorname{tan}⁡0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1,0⟩ \\  & =f(0)\end{aligned}
$$

So $\displaystyle \lim_{t \rightarrow t_0} \mathbf f (t) = \mathbf f (t_0)$ and therefore $\mathbf f (t)$ is continuous at $t=0.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Value of a Vector Function Using Properties of Continuous Functions
canonical_examples.problem:
Find $\mathbf g(1)$ given that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are two continuous vector-valued functions for which $\mathbf f(1) = \left\langle 1, 1, -1 \right\rangle$ and 

$$
\lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 1} \big[ 2\mathbf f(t)-\mathbf g(t) \big] = \left\langle 2, 1, -1 \right\rangle.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the constant multiple rule and the addition rule for limits, and the fact that both functions are continuous, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}[2f(t)-g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 1}2f(t)+{lim}_{t\to 1}[-g(t)] \\  & =2{lim}_{t\to 1}f(t)-{lim}_{t\to 1}g(t) \\  & =2f(1)-g(1) \\  & =2{{⟨1,1,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{f(1)}-g(1) \\  & =⟨2,2,-2⟩-g(1).\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, we are told that

$$
\lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 1} \big[ 2\mathbf f(t)-\mathbf g(t) \big] = \left\langle 2, 1, -1 \right\rangle.
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following equation which we can solve for $\mathbf{g} (1)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 1}[2f(t)-g(t)] & =⟨2,1,-1⟩ \\ ⟨2,2,-2⟩-g(1) & =⟨2,1,-1⟩ \\ g(1) & =⟨2,2,-2⟩-⟨2,1,-1⟩ \\ g(1) & =⟨0,1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Differentiability of a Vector Function
canonical_examples.problem: Is the vector function $\mathbf{f}(t) = \left\langle 2e^t, \: \dfrac{\pi}{t-3}, \: \sqrt{t} \right\rangle$ differentiable with respect to $t$ on $t \in [0, 2]?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function is defined on $t \in [0, 2].$ Remember that a function is differentiable on the interval $[0, 2]$ if and only if all of its component functions are differentiable on that interval.

Let's now differentiate $\mathbf f(t)$ to find $\mathbf f'(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\pi }{t-3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{t},\,-\frac{\pi }{(t-3)^{2}},\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the third component of this vector, $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}$ is undefined at $t = 0.$ Therefore, we conclude that the function $\mathbf f(t)$ is **not** differentiable on $[0,2].$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Interval on Which a Product of Functions is Differentiable
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the interval where the function $\mathbf g(t)\cdot\mathbf h(t)$ is differentiable,  given the following functions $\mathbf g(t)$ and $\mathbf h(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j-\sqrt{t}\,k \\ h(t) & =2t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function $\mathbf F(t) = \mathbf g(t)\cdot\mathbf h(t)$ is differentiable over the common domain where both $\mathbf g(t)$ and $\mathbf h(t)$ are differentiable. Remember that a vector function is differentiable if and only if each component is differentiable.

So, let's start by finding the intervals where each of the functions $\mathbf g(t)$ and $\mathbf h(t)$ are differentiable.

For the function $\mathbf g(t)\mathbin{:}$ 

- The first component, $3\sin t,$ and  the second component, $-\cos(2t),$ are  differentiable over $(-\infty, \infty).$

- The third component $- \sqrt t$ is differentiable on $(0, \infty).$ Its derivative is not defined at $t=0$ and the function is not defined for $t <0.$

The intersection of the intervals of differentiability of all three components of $\mathbf g(t)$ is $(0,\infty).$  So, $\mathbf g(t)$ is differentiable on $(0,\infty).$

For the function $\mathbf h(t)\mathbin{:}$ 

- All three component functions are defined and are differentiable for all values of $t \in (-\infty, \infty).$ 

So, $\mathbf h(t)$ is differentiable on $(-\infty, \infty).$

Finally, the common domain of differentiability for $\mathbf g(t)$ and $\mathbf h(t)$  is $(0, \infty) \cap (-\infty, \infty) =  (0,\infty).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding Singular Value Decomposition
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/78735529c93fa6286edc0fdc69d7398ec9cf758f7e46a0fb71702300aadbeb19.png)
Consider the matrix $U$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of a $2\times2$ matrix $A,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $U?$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/703a545742438a81183008b90c0336ee51e9fc230d72ed44b02dbd76f0292f7f.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that since $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of a $2\times2$ matrix $A,$ the matrix $U$ must be a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the first column must be orthogonal to the second column, and

- the norm of the second column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Columns of the Third Matrix Given Part of a Singular Value Decomposition
canonical_examples.problem:

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|v_{11}|+|v_{21}|?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that the singular values are $\sigma_1=5$ and $\sigma_2=3.$ So, the first column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value $\sigma_1=5.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of $A^T \!A$ corresponding to $\lambda_1 = \sigma_1^2=25.$ Computing $A^T \! A - 25 I,$ we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/be2d743322a536fc213e7e2a00a04c2b902ab15efafedd8a7e6f7935cd5c7592.png)

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T\!A-25I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/1f537b8ae115d1d01a03766d9c2006ca8bbee77e1b99228466642c5e89c0d0ef.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm, we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/77be4b42f9c5a8b379de6a74088106b6374bf28c48e9a7ceb2beb55d483afafe.png)

Therefore,

$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Columns of the First Matrix Given Part of a Singular Value Decomposition
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/ea3e5c13d236a733350a1d23b8629cd481f9316e16ab7558873e305fe198eb98.png)
Consider the matrices $A,$ $\Sigma,$ and $V$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the second column of $U?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ and $\sigma_i \neq 0,$ then the $i$th column of $U$ can be found as

$$
\mathbf{u}_i = \dfrac{1}{\sigma_i} A\mathbf{v}_i,
$$

 

where $\mathbf v_i$ is the $i$th column of the matrix $V.$

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that the singular values are $\sigma_1=9$ and $\sigma_2=4.$ Therefore, the second column of $U$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}6 & -5 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{12}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: The Singular Value Decomposition of a 2x2 Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/4d6b11d3095c2f0d39493b5ff95c16b3f7581938ced3e3eb6daa4daeacf74d55.png)
Consider the matrices $A$ and $\Sigma$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$  find the matrices $U$ and $V.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}-3 & 8 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 8 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 8 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -24 \\ -24 & 73\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=9$ and $\sigma_2=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \! A$):

- For $\lambda_1=\sigma_1^2=81,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-81I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -24 \\ -24 & 73\end{aligned}]-81[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-72 & -24 \\ -24 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 81I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives a unit eigenvector
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/296fe06c266dbb9b46bcd640204527e906be5d8a1c25aa371ff042b72e070eeb.png)

- For $\lambda_2=\sigma_2^2=1,$ we have

$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Possible Roots of a Polynomial Using the Rational Roots Theorem
canonical_examples.problem:
According to the rational roots theorem, which of the following could be a root of the polynomial $f(x) = 9x^4-3x^2-7x-6?$

- $-\dfrac{2}{3}$

- $\dfrac{3}{2}$

- $-9$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \dfrac{\textrm{factor of the constant term}}{\textrm{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-6,$ and the leading coefficient is $9.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \dfrac{\textrm{factor of }{-6}}{\textrm{factor of }9}.
$$

Of the given answer choices, only $-\dfrac{2}{3}$ takes the above form since the numerator $(2)$ is a factor of $-6$ and the denominator $(3)$ is a factor of $9.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Non-Roots of a Polynomial Using the Rational Roots Theorem
canonical_examples.problem:
According to the rational roots theorem, which of the following **cannot** be a root of the polynomial $f(x) = 12x^4+5x^3-6x+15?$

- $\dfrac{2}{3}$

- $\dfrac{1}{3}$

- $-\dfrac{3}{4}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \dfrac{\textrm{factor of the constant term}}{\textrm{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $15$ and the leading coefficient is $12.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \dfrac{\textrm{factor of }{15}}{\textrm{factor of }12}.
$$

Of the given answer choices, only $\dfrac 23$ does not take the above form. The numerator $(2)$ is not a factor of $15.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Counting the Number of Possible Rational Roots of a Polynomial
canonical_examples.problem: For the polynomial $f(x)=6x^4-7x^3+11x-9,$ how many *potential* roots are given by the rational roots theorem?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \dfrac{\textrm{factor of the constant term}}{\textrm{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial:

- The constant term is $-9,$ and its factors are $\pm1,$ $\pm3,$ and $\pm9.$

- The leading coefficient is $6,$ and its factors are $\pm 1,$ $\pm 2,$ $\pm 3,$ and $\pm 6.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{3}, & \pm \frac{1}{6}, \\ \pm \frac{3}{1}, & \pm \frac{3}{2}, & \pm \frac{3}{3}, & \pm \frac{3}{6}, \\ \pm \frac{9}{1}, & \pm \frac{9}{2}, & \pm \frac{9}{3}, & \pm \frac{9}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{3}, & \pm \frac{1}{6}, \\ \pm 3, & \pm \frac{3}{2}, & \pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, \\ \pm 9, & \pm \frac{9}{2}, & \pm 3, & \pm \frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that several potential roots are duplicates (shown above in red). Removing these duplicates, and listing those remaining in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\pm \frac{1}{6}, \; \pm \frac13, \; \pm \frac12, \; \pm 1, \; \pm \frac32, \; \pm 3, \; \pm \frac{9}{2}, \; \pm 9.
$$

This makes a total of $16$ potential roots. (Remember that each $\pm$ sign accounts for $2$ roots, and $2 \cdot 8 = 16.$)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Factoring a Cubic Polynomial Using the Rational Roots Theorem
canonical_examples.problem: Given that the polynomial $f(x) =x^3 - x^2 - 4x + 4$ has a root in the interval $(0,4),$ find the sum of the distinct real roots of $f(x).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \dfrac{\textrm{factor of the constant term}}{\textrm{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $4$ and the leading coefficient is $1.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \dfrac{\textrm{factor of }{4}}{\textrm{factor of }1}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm1, \pm 2, \pm 4
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(0,4),$ are $1$ and $2.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $\left(x-1\right)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | $x^3$ | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-4$ | $4$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-4$ |
|  | $1$ | $0$ | $-4$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $\left(x-1\right)$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x) = \left( x - 1\right) (x^2 - 4).
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-1)({x}^{2}-4) \\  & =(x-1)(x+2)(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=-2, 1, 2.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
-2+1+2 =1.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Vector Fields That Satisfy the Unit Curl Property
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
\displaystyle \oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}
$$

 
represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ which of the following could be the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)?$

- $\left\langle -y, \: y\right\rangle$

- $\left\langle -2x, \: 2x\right\rangle$

- $\left\langle 5y\sin x, \: x-5\cos x \right\rangle$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
According to Green's theorem, if $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle P(x,y), \: Q(x,y) \right\rangle,$ where

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Vector field I gives the required area. In this case, 
$\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = -1$
and
$\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = 0,$
which gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 1.
$$

- Vector field II does not give the required area. In this case, 
$\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0$
and
$\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = 2,$
which gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 2.
$$

- Vector field III gives the required area. Notice that
$\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 5\sin x$
and
$\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} = 1+5\sin x,$
which gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle 2\sin t, \: 2 \cos t \rangle$ for $t \in \left [0, 2\pi \right).$ 
The area of $D$ can be written as

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095064/assets/b6cfc404b1866e7791c2a2e120133d5bb4c3bf586e9b3aadfda62042e70478b9.png)

where $P(x,y) = -y$ and $Q(x,y) = 0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

*Hint: Note that $C$ is negatively oriented.*

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095064/assets/a5eeb5db90f9ee0d86a49e5bbf02629c7886fa019db7cff3c4d0e1eb43e8fd75.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0 - \left(-1\right) = 1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y) = -y$ and $Q(x,y) = 0,$ we get

$$
- \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = \oint\limits_C y \: \text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is

$$
\mathbf{r}'(t) = \left\langle  2\cos t ,\:  -2 \sin t \right\rangle.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing expression is $4\cos^2 t.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating an Area Using Green's Theorem
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C=C_1 \cup C_2,$ where 

- $C_1$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}_1(t) =-2 t^4 \: \mathbf{i} + t^3 \: \mathbf{j}$ for $t \in \left[-1,1\right],$ and

- $C_2$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}_2(t) = -2\: \mathbf{i} -t \: \mathbf{j}$ for $t \in \left[-1,1\right].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095064/assets/147e8fdd97fc938ae5482b70d7215483956a860ee3ce69ae5bbebd111dcc343b.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0 - \left(-1\right) = 1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y) = -y$ and $Q(x,y) = 0,$ we get

$$
\oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = -\oint\limits_C y \: \text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivatives of $\mathbf r_1(t)$ and $\mathbf r_2(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=-8{t}^{3}\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}}y\,dx-{∮}_{{C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{3}\cdot (-8{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-t)\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{6}\,\text{d}t+0 \\  & =8[\frac{{t}^{7}}{7}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =8\cdot \frac{2}{7} \\  & =\frac{16}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Columns of the First Matrix Given Part of an SVD With a Zero Eigenvalue
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095079/assets/cc3969660197510f4c7abb016b6d4ed593b8eb69e59fc9b1396c4c1ddcc1e549.png)
Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the second column of $U?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ and $\sigma_i \neq 0,$ then the $i$th column of $U$ can be found as

$$
\mathbf{u}_i = \dfrac{1}{\sigma_i} A\mathbf{v}_i,
$$

 

where $\mathbf u_i$ and $\mathbf v_i$ are the $i$th columns of the orthogonal matrices $U$ and $V,$ respectively.  

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that the singular values are $\sigma_1=2\sqrt{2}$ and $\sigma_2=0.$ Therefore, the first column of $U$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & -1 \\ -\sqrt{3} & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is $\sigma_2=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095079/assets/e0566311c99934171da98a96e1bed902588698ac948f817cea20d98920e64581.png)

such that 

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0 \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \|\mathbf{u}_2\|=1.
$$

 

Solving $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} x_1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} x_2 = 0,
$$

we get a nonzero solution ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095079/assets/e6415e2bc0b61c20486c61216ca322e3bdc0e6efb9ae2570c2b255b898225432.png) Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the  second column of $U\mathbin{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095079/assets/f053fd32c444f585085929ac6908e1d2bc66fb4dad71bdf64c6498a026f9d237.png)

Consider the matrices $A$ and $\Sigma$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the matrices $U$ and $V.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}32 & -16 \\ -16 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=2\sqrt{10}$ and $\sigma_2=0.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \! A$):

- For $\lambda_1=\sigma_1^2=40,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-40I & =[\begin{aligned}32 & -16 \\ -16 & 8\end{aligned}]-40[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8 & -16 \\ -16 & -32\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 40I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives a unit eigenvector
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095079/assets/1c07efd18aff72d18dc8725832e33160c001e0d441b0ef0748a519389ea1bff4.png)

- For $\lambda_2=\sigma_2^2=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}32 & -16 \\ -16 & 8\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}32 & -16 \\ -16 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 0I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives a unit eigenvector
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095079/assets/14bda31a91349b26190594065760f44f14e329f648b7e5f8a6d84c03d803ee4b.png)

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since the first singular value is not zero, and we know the corresponding singular right vector, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{10}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{10}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is $\sigma_2=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095079/assets/1b0599cec4f025662f6f98b17952bd0e039d59a93fa2a7914067a74e4622f793.png)
such that 

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0 \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \|\mathbf{u}_2\|=1.
$$

 

Solving $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} x_1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} x_2 = 0,
$$

we get a nonzero solution ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095079/assets/34e66b511d6b341028b98d3676de1672feef643210fc0fe146969e0b3f73b542.png) Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the  second column of $U\mathbin{:}$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095079/assets/54448d8e2782a9be652cbc492c5d0f570de360a82f2913e8bc81bdec6c333cc1.png)

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$: Seeking non-zero solutions of $(A^T\!A-2I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0},$ we obtain the unit eigenvectors 

$\qquad$ ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095079/assets/a41a31eedadef820e4ba39ff9219723b663967a70546d2b845f17a527ad5d2c7.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095079/assets/403e2da8a3f4686091140b901d53679de7adb76210df2ba836288e1ebe15683f.png)

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\textrm{Var}[4k^2-1]$ where $k$ is a constant.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that for any constant $a,$ we have

$$
\textrm{Var}[a] = 0.

$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Variance of a Scaled Random Variable
canonical_examples.problem:
The probability distribution of the random variable $X$ is given below. Given that $\textrm E[X] = 2.3,$ calculate $\textrm{Var}[-10X].$ 

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ | $0.5$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constant $a,$ we have

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX] = a^2\cdot\textrm{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=-10.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[-10X] & =(-10)^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =100\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm E[X^2] - \textrm E[X]^2
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\textrm E [X] =2.3.$ 

We start by computing $\textrm E[X^2].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X^2$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(3) \\  & =1(0.2)+4(0.3)+9(0.5) \\  & =5.9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =5.9-{(2.3)}^{2} \\  & =0.61.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[-10X] & =100\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =100\cdot 0.61 \\  & =61.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Variance of a Transformed Random Variable
canonical_examples.problem: If $\textrm{Var}[X] = 10,$ calculate $\textrm{Var}[1-2X].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constants $a$ and $b,$ we have

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX+b] = a^2\cdot\textrm{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=-2$ and $b=1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[1-2X] & =(-2)^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =4\cdot 10 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Carrying Capacity for the Prey
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=6x(1-0.1x)-3xy \\ {y}^{′}=-7y+5xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the modified Lotka-Volterra model, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Find the maximum carrying capacity for the prey in the case of the complete absence of predators.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity is given by

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants. Here, $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

In our case, the equation describing the dynamics of the prey is given by

$$
x' = 6x(1-0.1x) - 3xy
$$

where 

- the $6x(1-0.1x)$ term defines the growth, and

- the $-3xy$ term defines the decay due to interaction with predators.

In the case of the complete absence of predators, we have $y = 0,$ and this equation becomes

$$
x' = 6x(1-0.1x).
$$

General solutions to this equation are logistic functions with two horizontal asymptotes defined by the equilibrium solutions, which can be found by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x(1-0.1x)=0\,⇒\,x=0,\,10\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibria are $x=0$ and $x=10.$ The nonzero equilibrium gives the maximum capacity.

Therefore, the maximum carrying capacity for the prey in the case of the complete absence of predators is $10.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Equilibrium Points of the Modified Lotka-Volterra System
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=5x(1-0.2x)-4xy \\ {y}^{′}=-6y+3xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Find the equilibria of the model.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}5x(1-0.2x)-4xy=0 \\ -6y+3xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6y+3xy & =0 \\ y(-6+3x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=2.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5x(1-0.2x)-4x(0) & =0 \\ 5x(0.2x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $(5,0).$

- If $x=2,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5(2)(1-0.2(2))-(4)(2)y & =0 \\ 10(1-0.4)-8y & =0 \\ 10(0.6)-8y & =0 \\ 6-8y & =0 \\ y & =0.75.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(2, 0.75).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0), \qquad
(5, 0), \qquad
(2, 0.75).
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Stable Case
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity below, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=5x(1-x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-y+2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[0.5, \, 2.5]^T,$ and classify this equilibrium point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=5x(1-x)-xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-y+2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5x(1-x)-xy)=5-10x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5x(1-x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y+2xy)=2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y+2xy)=-1+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095078/assets/b046e51c9a1b68cc22e1bd46f532a8d8d70452e5549937aaa8d872e60c63eb20.png)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095078/assets/e91d26ba55bafc85ce58c65482858d3f2094136b9620fe5d6a30b514ffe59b87.png) to get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095078/assets/dcdb4709be5d408bf054292b36e9bd898db3047b4c66230fc9249fc57e229b2b.png)

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-2.5-\lambda  & -0.5 \\ 5 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2.5-\lambda )(-\lambda )-5(-0.5) & =0 \\ \lambda (2.5+\lambda )+2.5 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2.5\lambda +2.5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues $\lambda_{1,2} = -1.25 \pm 0.25\sqrt{15}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are complex with negative real parts, our equilibrium is an asymptotically stable spiral sink.
