canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Rate of Change of the Area Given the Rate of Change of the Side Length
canonical_examples.problem:
Each side of a square is decreasing at a rate of $2\,\text{cm/min}.$ How fast is the area of the square decreasing when the sides are $10\,\text{cm}?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/a06eb0963dc6d01e45acb9349e5232ba70a11c98c99ee63c2ec0dae3d748f5ed.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} .
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A = x^2.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is decreasing at a rate of $2\,\text{cm/min},$ so we have $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} = -2.$ Also, when the sides are $10\,\text{cm},$ we have $x=10.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =(-2)\cdot 2(10)=-40{\text{ cm}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square decreases at a rate of $40\,\text{cm}^2/\text{min}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding an Expression for the Rate of Change of a Side Length Given the Rate of Change of the Area
canonical_examples.problem: The area of a square decreases at a rate of $20 \text{ cm}^2\text{/s}.$ If $x$ and $A$ denote the side length and area of the square respectively, then find an expression for $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
This situation is different. Here, the *area* is changing at a constant rate,  and we want to know the rate at which the side lengths are changing.

First, let's draw a diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/f4125cebd7553bb8b106a8baff39a6e4a120b9d9e5cdf2c4c9c0a9a676558897.png)

We want to find $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}.$ The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A = x^2.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We know from the given information that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-20\text{ cm[math]^2[/math]/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this information, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}-20 & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{10}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Relating the Rate of Change of a Diagonal Length to Another Rate of Change
canonical_examples.problem: The sides of a square are increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the square is numerically equal to twice the rate of increase of the diagonal. What is the area of the square at that moment?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A = \dfrac{h^2}{2}.
$$

Using implicit differentiation and the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = 2\dfrac{\textrm d h}{\textrm d t}$, so replacing $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm dt}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =h\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ 2\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} & =h\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} \\ 2 & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

So at that particular moment, we have $h=2,$ and therefore the area of the square at that moment is

$$
A = \dfrac{2^2}{2} = 2.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Rate of Change of Area Given a Rate of Change of a Diagonal: Word Problem
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/2677121139896da73eca5277c7c23f193467001eabba976cb48b2232f4bcbad6.png)

In a testing facility, a scientist is increasing the diagonals of a simple square at a rate of $12 \text{ mm}\text{/min}.$ At what rate, in squared millimeters per minute, is the area of the square increasing when the length of the diagonal is $6\, \text{mm}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $h$ and $A$ be the length of the diagonals and the area of the square, respectively. Using the Pythagorean theorem, it can be shown that the relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A = \dfrac{h^2}{2}.
$$

We want to find

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $h$ increases at a rate of $12\,\textrm{mm/min},$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we want to compute the rate of change of the area when the diagonal has length $h=6.$ Substituting this information into our expression for $\dfrac{\textrm{d}A}{\textrm d t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =12\cdot 6=72{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Listing the Elements in a Power Set
canonical_examples.problem: Find $\mathcal{P}(A)$ if $A = \{ 2, 4, \{ 8 \} \}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The power set of $A,$ denoted $\mathcal{P}(A),$ is the set that contains every possible subset of $A,$ including the empty set $\emptyset.$

So, let's list all possible subsets of $A$ using a tree diagram.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095809/assets/b3af256806e0aeb0396564320800f908c66d5830ab46e676dfc51ceab24154f6.png)

According to our diagram, the subsets of $A$ are

$$
\emptyset = \{\},\quad \{2\},\quad \{4\},\quad \{ \{8\} \}, \quad \{2, 4\},\quad \{2, \{8\}\},\quad \{4, \{8\}\},\quad\{2, 4, \{8\}\}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\mathcal{P}(A) = \{\emptyset, \{2\}, \{4\}, \{\{8\}\}, \{2, 4\}, \{2, \{8\}\}, \{4, \{8\}\},\{2, 4, \{8\}\}\}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Cardinality of a Power Set
canonical_examples.problem: If $Y = \{ 1, \{ 3, 5 \}, 7, X \},$ then what is $\left|\mathcal{P}(Y)\right|?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For any set $Y,$ we have $\left|\mathcal{P}(Y)\right| = 2^{\left| Y \right|}.$

In this case, $\left| Y \right| = 4,$ so we have

$$
\left| \mathcal{P}(Y) \right| = 2^{\left| Y \right|} = 2^{4} = 16.
$$

Remember that $\{ 3,5 \}$ is a single element in the set $Y.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining Cardinality in More Advanced Cases
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $Y =\{\mu\}$ and $Z =\{1,2\},$ find $\left|\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(Y\times Z))\right|.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For any set $S,$ we have $\left|\mathcal{P}(S)\right| = 2^{\left| S \right|}.$ Also, $|S \times T| = |S| \cdot |T|.$

In our case, 

$$
\left| Y \right| = 1, \qquad
\left| Z \right| = 2.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}|P(Y\times Z)| & ={2}^{|Y\times Z|} \\  & ={2}^{|Y|\,\cdot \,|Z|} \\  & ={2}^{1\cdot 2} \\  & ={2}^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|P(P(Y\times Z))| & ={2}^{|P(Y\times Z)|} \\  & ={2}^{4} \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- $\mathcal{P}(\{\{\emptyset\}\})  = \{ \emptyset, \{\emptyset\} \}$

- $\mathcal{P} (\{ \emptyset, \{0\} \} ) = \{ \emptyset, \{0\}, \{\{\emptyset\}\}, \{0, \emptyset\} \}$

- $\mathcal{P}( \mathcal{P}(\{y\}))  = \{ \emptyset, \{\emptyset\}, \{\{y\}\}, \{\emptyset, \{y\}\} \}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The power set of $T,$ denoted $\mathcal{P}(T),$ is the set that contains every possible subset of $T,$ including the empty set $\emptyset.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Notice that we are given the set $\{\{\emptyset\}\}.$ So, its power set must be $\{ \emptyset, \{\{\emptyset\}\} \}.$

- Statement II is false. Notice that we are given the set $\{ \emptyset, \{0\} \} .$ So, its power set must be $\{ \emptyset, \{\{0\}\}, \{\emptyset\}, \{\emptyset, \{0\} \} \}.$

- Statement III is true. Notice that we are given the set $\{y\}.$ So, its power set must be $\{\emptyset, \{y\} \}.$ Therefore, $\mathcal{P}( \mathcal{P}(\{y\})) = \{ \emptyset, \{\emptyset\}, \{\{y\}\}, \{\emptyset, \{y\}\} \}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Writing a Complex Number in Exponential Form
canonical_examples.problem: Write the complex number $z=4+4\textrm{i}$ in exponential form.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To write our complex number in the form $z = r\textrm{e}^{\textrm{i}\theta},$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta = \arg(z),$ we first calculate $r\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z$ lies in the first quadrant of the complex plane, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=4\sqrt{2}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ into $z=re^{\textrm{i}\theta},$ we get

$$
z = 4\sqrt{2}\,\textrm{e}^{\pi\textrm{i}/4}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying the Missing Set to Form a Partition
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the set $X = \{ -4, -1, 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17 \}.$ Which subset must be placed into the blank in the set below so that it represents a partition of $X?$

$$
\{ \{ -1, 5, 8 \}, \{ -4, 11 \}, \{ 14 \}, \, \_\_\_\_ \, \}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A partition of a set $X$ is a collection of non-empty subsets of $X$ where every element of $X$ is contained in *exactly* one subset. 

In order to find the subset that goes in the blank, we must identify which elements of $X$ are not yet contained within any of the given subsets.

Let's go through each element of $X$ and check:

- $-4 \in \{ -4, 11 \} \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

- $-1 \in \{ -1, 5, 8 \} \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

- $2$ does not belong to any of the given subsets $\quad \color{red}\times$

- $5 \in \{ -1, 5, 8 \} \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

- $8 \in \{ -1, 5, 8 \} \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

- $11 \in \{ -4, 11 \} \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

- $14 \in \{ 14 \} \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

- $17$ does not belong to any of the given subsets $\quad \color{red}\times$

The elements $2$ and $17$ are not yet contained within any of the given subsets. Therefore, the subset that must go in the blank is $\{ 2,17 \}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Partitions
canonical_examples.problem:
If $X = \{ a, b, c, d, e, f, g \},$ which of the following collections of subsets of $X$ are partitions of $X?$

- $\{ a, b, \{ c,d,e \}, \{ f,g \} \}$

- $\{ \{ a, b, c \}, \{ d,e,f \}, \{ g \} \}$

- $\{ \emptyset, \{ a,b,c \}, \{ f,g \} \}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A partition of a set $X$ is a collection of non-empty subsets of $X$ where every element of $X$ is contained in *exactly* one subset. 

With that in mind, let's inspect each collection of subsets.

- Collection I is *not* a partition because $a$ and $b$ are not subsets.

- Collection II is a partition. All the subsets are non-empty, and every element of $X$ is contained in exactly one subset.

- Collection III is *not* a partition. The subset $\emptyset$ is empty, and the elements $d$ and $e$ do not appear in any subsets.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Mapping an Area to a Rectangular Region: Transformations Given
canonical_examples.problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u = \dfrac{y^2}{x}, \qquad v= xy,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
x = {y^2}, \qquad x=\dfrac{y^2}3, \qquad y=\dfrac2x, \qquad y=\dfrac4x.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/e4acf61532998ca5b0768b7edde16be779298c1be15ef11b14472678ba43043a.png)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u = \dfrac{y^2}{x}, \qquad v= xy
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/3706f0373bb39ebd41d78dd453896548ec03638a656e1fe36604f2a43108ba8e.png)

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u= \dfrac{y^2}{x}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & x={y}^{2} & ⟹\, & \frac{{y}^{2}}{x}=1 & ⟹\, & u=1 \\  & x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{3} & ⟹\, & \frac{{y}^{2}}{x}=3 & ⟹\, & u=3\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v = xy$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{2}{x} & ⟹\, & xy=2 & ⟹\, & v=2 \\  & y=\frac{4}{x} & ⟹\, & xy=4 & ⟹\, & v=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 1 \leq u \leq 3, \quad 2 \leq v \leq 4\big\}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/1207d8cdb8afd7c55d712caca043edfe9f0d0395343a6cbd329cf5861ec3bce7.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{2y}{x} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{aligned}| \\  & =-\frac{3{y}^{2}}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = -\dfrac{x}{3y^2} = -\dfrac{1}{3u}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{3u}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\cdot (4-2) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Mapping an Area to a Rectangular Region: Transformations Not Given
canonical_examples.problem:
Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the following curves.

$$
e^y = \dfrac{5}{e^x}, \qquad e^y=\dfrac{10}{e^x}, \qquad e^x=e^y, \qquad e^x=2e^y
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/f47c1b7ce7e9073a10c2665821a4fc0d5b38ce6ad6c0f79a75a5b203962112cd.png)

We'll assume this transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v,
$$

  

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

To compute the required area, we proceed in five steps:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

Notice that we can rewrite the equations of our curves as follows:

$$
e^{x+y} = 5, \qquad e^{x+y}=10, \qquad e^{x-y} = 1, \qquad e^{x-y} = 2
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u = e^{x+y}, \qquad v = e^{x-y}
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/88c92ebc206481c3ef86661ee413358bb060cb85f642148c609de0bf1a9da2d1.png)

**Step 2**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=e^{x+y}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {e}^{x+y}=5\,⟹\,u=5 \\  & {e}^{x+y}=10\,⟹\,u=10\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v =e^{x-y}$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {e}^{x-y}=1\,⟹\,v=1 \\  & {e}^{x-y}=2\,⟹\,v=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 5 \leq u \leq 10, \quad 1 \leq v \leq 2\big\}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/105745a82e8f67b086f526b0166e3b442d3eaf02e4df69314ed9d3ffd5fca071.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+y} & {e}^{x+y} \\ {e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =-{e}^{2x}-{e}^{2x} \\  & =-2{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} =  -\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-2x}=-\dfrac{1}{2uv}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)}\neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 5**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{2uv}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{uv}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{5}^{10}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡10-\operatorname{ln}⁡5)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding an Area by Transforming to a Type I Region
canonical_examples.problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u =3x-2y, \quad v=x+y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(3x-2y)^2 - y - x = 0$ and the line $x+y=4.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/87b44aa661a51ee39011c33c2eb000edcebb127508d45d5819339cf532258f3e.png)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u = 3x-2y, \qquad v=x+y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/88c92ebc206481c3ef86661ee413358bb060cb85f642148c609de0bf1a9da2d1.png)

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $3x-2y = u$ and $x+y = v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x-2y)^{2}-y-x=0\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x + y = v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y+x=4\,⟹\,v=4.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{2} \\ v=4\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm 2 \\ v=4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 2, 4).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: -2 \leq u \leq 2, \, u^2 \leq v \leq 4\big\},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/0a3d0211dfbe18e5737b62e8b61cf9308af2735ef827d14bae7b5dbfffaa4faa.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = (5)^{-1} = \dfrac 15.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}[{\int }_{{u}^{2}}^{4}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}[v]_{{u}^{2}}^{4}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot 2{\int }_{0}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{[4u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(8-\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{32}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Image of a Point or Segment
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/2abec0420bf322120bb37135af682a7bc04c97c86d7bf1bdfd04012a8355883c.png)

Consider the segment $\overline{PQ}$ above, and the transformation $\mathbf T$ defined as

$$
x = u - v + 7, \qquad y = u + v +1.
$$

The image of $\overline{PQ}$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ is the segment $\overline{P'Q'}$ in the $xy$-plane. Find $\overline{P'Q'}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that we can express the given transformation as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v+7 \\ u+v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $\mathbf T$ maps the endpoints of $\overline{PQ}$ to the endpoints of $\overline{P'Q'}.$ So, to find the image of $\overline{PQ},$ we find the images of each endpoint.

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing the endpoints of our segment:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/faf8bd29c9813cf0f73fca4b58f5636d3eb3262eae64ac099bdcdc569096ab0c.png)

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $\mathbf b$ in each column:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/074650a4370dd709462de2400991a1d7ec0e8279ea4e7e414bf956e511f7cace.png)

The image of $\mathbf u$ under $\mathbf T$ is given by $A\mathbf u + \mathbf b.$ So, by applying $\mathbf T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}7 & 7 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -10 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}7 & 7 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the endpoints of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(0,-2)$ and $(-3,1).$

Drawing this region in the $xy$-plane, we get the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/61508357c514f50b27498bee50dce36d22b7f55f0baf8c2d6a58ad2d53dc879d.png)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Image of a Polygon Under an Affine Transformation
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/dd8b1407add93e72afccf2138cc818df63d47fdaa6ccc23e843a5602d8c1dbd8.png)

          

Consider the rectangle $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
\Delta  = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: -1 \leq u \leq 1, \: -1\leq v \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

The transformation $\mathbf T$ is defined as

$$
x = u - v + 1, \qquad y = u+v
$$

Find the image of $\Delta$ in the $xy$-plane under the action of $\mathbf T.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that we can express the given transformation as 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v+1 \\ u+v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $\mathbf T$ maps the boundary of $\Delta$ to the boundary of the image. So, to find the image of $\Delta,$ we find the images of each side.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/69d92e24d5b0c81e54d3878793efe7c07d16fc963222997fe4fec4ffb3f93bd5.png)

          

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing all vertices of our square:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/047cd6bf2960418919b4a11ae6920d9fc589881062ddbb3eed918116a7e4c4fd.png)

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $\mathbf b$ in each column:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/cfc1c3e72dd7764d9835e35f1943ef96c6829703ca8f0b2bce67153df9df88e5.png)

The image of $\mathbf u$ under $T$ is given by $A\mathbf u + \mathbf b.$ So, by applying $\mathbf T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertices of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(1,-2), (3,0), (1,2),$ and $(-1,0).$

Drawing this region in the $xy$-plane, we get the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/ddd14bdebe21c830396e044721811cf6b9c7bd7db067e4d0ff7d35e02a592894.png)

          

Notice that since $\det(A) = 2 >    0,$ this transformation is orientation-preserving.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining Whether an Affine Transformation is Orientation-Preserving
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T$ defined as

$$
x = v - u-6, \qquad y = v -2u  .
$$

Let $A$ be the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/af7ea1dee03533df623aef652cc2eb8cc7590647ef10652163e14d3a322f7b7f.png)

- $\det(A) = 1$

- The transformation $\mathbf T$ is orientation-preserving
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}v-u-6 \\ v-2u\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-u+v \\ -2u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T$ is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/6522a8eb76f3ff239aefdd3c7aff95ddfedbc5deb8be854002643afba4b94411.png)

- Statement II is true. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/aadc5c7a23fd39c8329d35a3b9befdd0eb48b2e97e4122744d1a4e19e0ce45d6.png)

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $\det(A) > 0,$ the affine transformation $\mathbf T$ is orientation-preserving.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Sum of a Geometric Series
canonical_examples.problem: Compute the sum of the first $7$ terms of the geometric series $3+6+12+\cdots$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a geometric series, the sum of the first $N$ terms is given by the formula

$$
S_N = a_1\dfrac{(1-r^N)}{1-r},
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term of the series and $r$ is the common ratio.

In our case, $a_1 = 3.$ To find the value of $r,$ we find the ratio of the first two terms in the series:

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{6}{3} = 2
$$

If we substitute $a_1 = 3,$ $N = 7,$ and $r = 2$ into our formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{7} & =3\cdot \frac{1-{2}^{7}}{1-2} \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1-{2}^{7}}{-1} \\  & =-3(-127) \\  & =381.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Sum of a Geometric Series With a Negative Common Ratio
canonical_examples.problem: Compute the sum of the first $6$ terms of the geometric series $2 -8 + 32 - 128 + \cdots$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a geometric series, the sum of the first $N$ terms is given by the formula

$$
S_N = a_1\dfrac{(1-r^N)}{1-r},
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term of the series and $r$ is the common ratio.

In our case, $a_1 = 2.$ To find the value of $r,$ we find the ratio of the first two terms in the series:

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{-8}{2} = -4
$$

If we substitute $a_1 = 2$ and $r = -4$ in the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{6} & =2\cdot \frac{1-(-4)^{6}}{1-(-4)} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1-{4}^{6}}{1+4} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{-4\,095}{5} \\  & =-1\,638.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Sum of a Geometric Series Given the Last Term of the Series
canonical_examples.problem:
What is the sum of the geometric series $1 + 6 + 36 + \cdots + 46\,656?$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that $46\,656 = 6^6.$*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The sum of the first $N$ terms of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
S_N = a_1\dfrac{(1-r^N)}{1-r},
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term of this series, and $r$ is the common ratio. In our case, we have $a_1 = 1.$

To find $r,$ we find the ratio of the consecutive terms $a_1$ and $a_2 \mathbin{:}$

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{6}{1} = 6
$$

Now we must determine $N$ (the index of the last term). To do this, we use the fact that

$$
a_N = a_1 \cdot r^{N-1} .
$$

Therefore, using the hint, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}46\,656 & =1\cdot {6}^{N-1} \\ 46\,656 & ={6}^{N-1} \\ {6}^{6} & ={6}^{N-1} \\ 6 & =N-1 \\ N & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, if we substitute $a_1 = 1,$ $r = 6,$ and $N = 7$ in the formula for $S_N,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{7} & =1\cdot \frac{1-{6}^{7}}{1-6} \\  & =\frac{{6}^{7}-1}{5} \\  & =\frac{279\,935}{5} \\  & =55\,987.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Sum of a Geometric Series Given Two Consecutive Terms of the Series
canonical_examples.problem: The second term of a geometric series is $20$ and the third term is $100.$ What is the sum of the first $6$ terms?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The sum of the first $N$ terms of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
S_N = a_1\dfrac{(1-r^N)}{1-r},
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term of the series, and $r$ is the common ratio.

To find $r,$ we find the ratio of the consecutive terms $a_2$ and $a_3 \mathbin{:}$

$$
r = \dfrac{a_3}{a_2} = \dfrac{100}{20} = 5
$$

Now we must determine the value of $a_1.$ To do this, we use the formula for the $n$th term, which states that

$$
a_n  = a_1 \cdot r^{n-1}.
$$

For $n = 2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {5}^{2-1} \\ 20 & ={a}_{1}\cdot 5 \\ {a}_{1} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, if we substitute $a_1 = 4,$ $N = 6,$ and $r = 5$ into the formula for $S_N,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{6} & =4\cdot \frac{1-{5}^{6}}{1-5} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1-{5}^{6}}{-4} \\  & ={5}^{6}-1 \\  & =15\,624.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Rate of Change of a Side Given the Rate of Change of the Volume
canonical_examples.problem:
A cube is shrinking uniformly at a rate of $3\,\text{mm}^3/\text{s}.$ How fast is each side of the cube shrinking when the volume of the cube is $27\,\text{mm}^3?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14096050/assets/0ca7021995b1a501f6cb862b33649bdb1927f7ce4a8630a9e261382a193f40a4.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side of the cube and $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-3\,{\text{mm}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm dt}$ when $V=27\,\text{mm}^3.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the cube:

$$
V=x^3
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Before we plug in the known values, we need to find the value of $x$ when $V = 27\,\text{mm}^3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={x}^{3} \\ 27 & ={x}^{3} \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug $x=3$ and $\dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm dt}=-3$ into the expression for $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm dt}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ -3 & =3(3)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\, \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sides of the cube are shrinking at a rate of $\dfrac{1}{9}\,\text{mm}/\text{s}$ at the moment when $x=3\,\textrm{mm}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Rate of Change of the Surface Area Given the Rate of Change of a Side (and Vice Versa)
canonical_examples.problem:
All of the edges of a cube are increasing at a rate of $2\,\text{mm}/\text{s}.$ How fast is the surface area of the cube changing when the volume of the cube is $8\,\text{cm}^3?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14096050/assets/a6ef2af1ed8e44f82469625e232ed67c0b809a3c8199a6ce52fd2bf2e3fcffa7.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side length of the cube, let $S$ be its surface area, and let $V$ be its volume. All of the variables change with time. In particular, we are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2\,\text{mm}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\dfrac{\textrm d S}{\textrm dt}$ when $V= 8\,\text{cm}^3.$

We want to find the rate of change of $S$ knowing the rate of change of $x.$ So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the cube:

$$
S= 6x^2
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}S & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Before we plug in the known values, we need to find the value of $x$ when $V= 8\,\text{cm}^3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={x}^{3} \\ 8 & ={x}^{3} \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So $x=2\,\text{cm}=20\,\text{mm}.$

We can now plug the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12(20)(2) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =480.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the cube's surface area is changing at a rate of  $480 \,\text{mm}^2/\text{s}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Rate of Change of the Volume Given the Rate of Change of a Side
canonical_examples.problem:
Water is being poured into a rectangular prism-shaped tank. The length and width of this tank are $20 \textrm{ ft}$ and $15 \textrm{ ft},$ respectively. If the height of the water increases at a rate of $\dfrac{1}{6}\,\textrm{ft/min}$, determine the rate at which the volume of stored water increases.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14096050/assets/ea7c6749ec0585ab714640fa9155eba212e2a9c628b50cc3c3de07492b8b3aec.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We define the following variables:

- let $L$ and $W$ be the length and width of the tank, respectively, and

- let $h$ and $V$ be the height and volume of the water in the tank, respectively.

Note that $h$ and $V$ change with time, while $L$ and $W$ are constants. 

We are given that

$$
L=20\,\text{ft}, \qquad  W=15\,\text{ft}, \qquad  \dfrac{\textrm dh}{\textrm dt} = \dfrac{1}{6}\,\text{ft}/\text{min}.
$$

We would like to find $\dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt}.$

The relation between the two time-dependent variables, $V$ and $h,$ is given by the formula for the volume of the water in the tank:

$$
V = LWh
$$

We differentiate both sides with respect to $t,$ treating both $L$ and $W$ as constants, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWh) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =LW\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(20)(15)\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =300\cdot \frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =50.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water level is rising at a rate of $50\,\text{ft}^3\textrm{/min}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Left or Right-Opening Parabola with Vertex at the Origin Given a Graph
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14096038/assets/70ff1c84aa4a9a2adc393fc1dcf684ee0bcf161671b15f9061e2319f5d7e0a39.png)

  

What is the equation of the parabola shown above?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that the arms of the parabola open to the left. The parabola has its vertex at $(0,0)$ and passes through the point $(-8,4).$

The general standard equation of a parabola whose vertex is $(0,0)$ and whose arms open right or left is given by

$$
y^2  = 4px.
$$

Since we know the given parabola passes through the point $(-8,4),$ we can substitute $x = -8$ and $y = 4$ into the standard equation and solve for $p\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4px \\ {4}^{2} & =4p(-8) \\ 16 & =-32p \\ p & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4px \\ {y}^{2} & =4(-\frac{1}{2})x \\ {y}^{2} & =-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the arms of the parabola open to the left since $p = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ is negative.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Left or Right-Opening Parabola with Vertex at the Origin Given Another Point
canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the right-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ and passes through the point $(4,4).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The general standard equation of a parabola whose vertex is $(0,0)$ and whose arms open right or left is given by

$$
y^2  = 4px.
$$

Since we know the given parabola passes through the point $(4,4),$ we can substitute $x=4$ and $y=4$ into the standard equation and solve for $p\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4px \\ {4}^{2} & =4p(4) \\ 16 & =16p \\ p & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4px \\ {y}^{2} & =4(1)x \\ {y}^{2} & =4x.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Left or Right-Opening Parabola Given a Graph
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14096038/assets/55651f756b31405e08cd96b097101528ffabff1e6411d3fcae9f40f747f607b4.png)

  

What is the equation of the parabola shown above?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the diagram we see that the arms of the parabola open to the left. The parabola has its vertex at $(4,2)$ and passes through the point $(0,6).$

The general standard equation of a parabola whose vertex is $(h, k)$ and whose arms open right or left is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-k)^{2} & =4p(x-h).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we know that the given parabola has its vertex at $(h, k) = (4,2),$ we substitute $h=4$ and $k=2$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-2)^{2} & =4p(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that the given parabola passes through the point $(0,6),$ so we can substitute $x=0$ and $y=6$ into the equation above and solve for $p\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-2)^{2} & =4p(x-4) \\ (6-2)^{2} & =4p(0-4) \\ 16 & =-16p \\ p & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-2)^{2} & =4p(x-4) \\ (y-2)^{2} & =4(-1)(x-4) \\ (y-2)^{2} & =-4(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the arms of the parabola open to the left since $p = -1$ is negative.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Left or Right-Opening Parabola Given the Vertex and Another Point
canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the left-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(2,-2)$ and passes through the point $(-6,2).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The general standard equation of a parabola whose vertex is $(h, k)$ and whose arms open right or left is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-k)^{2} & =4p(x-h).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we know that the given parabola has its vertex at $(h, k) = (2,-2),$ we substitute $h=2$ and $k=-2$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+2)^{2} & =4p(x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that the given parabola passes through the point $(-6, 2),$ so we can substitute $x=-6$ and $y=2$ into the equation above and solve for $p\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+2)^{2} & =4p(x-2) \\ (2+2)^{2} & =4p(-6-2) \\ 16 & =-32p \\ p & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+2)^{2} & =4p(x-2) \\ (y+2)^{2} & =4(-\frac{1}{2})(x-2) \\ (y+2)^{2} & =-2(x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Writing a Geometric Series Using Sigma Notation
canonical_examples.problem: Write the geometric series $4+ 12 + 36 +108+324$ using sigma notation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We must express the given series in the form

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{N}a_1 r^{n-1},
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term of the series, $r$ is the common ratio, and $N$ is the number of terms in the series. In this case, $a_1 = 4$ and $N = 5.$

To find $r,$ we calculate the ratio of the first two terms in the series:

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{12}{4} = 3
$$

Therefore, expressing the geometric series given in sigma notation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}4+12+36+108+324 & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}4\cdot {3}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Writing a Geometric Series Using Sigma Notation With Simplifications
canonical_examples.problem: Express the geometric series $4+8+16+32+64$ using sigma notation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we must express the given series in the form

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{N}a_1 r^{n-1},
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term of the series, $r$ is the common ratio, and $N$ is the number of terms in the series. In this case, $a_1 =4$ and $N = 5.$

To find $r,$ we calculate the ratio of the first two terms in the series:

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{8}{4} = 2
$$

Now, expressing the geometric series given in sigma notation, we obtain

$$
4+8+16+32+64 = \sum_{n=1}^{5}4  \cdot 2^{n - 1}.
$$

Finally, we can simplify the above series using the laws of exponents, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{5}4\cdot {2}^{n-1} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}4\cdot {2}^{n}\cdot {2}^{-1} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}4\cdot {2}^{n}\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}4\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {2}^{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}2\cdot {2}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Writing a Geometric Series With a Negative Common Ratio Using Sigma Notation
canonical_examples.problem: Write the geometric series $1 - 4 + 16 - 64 + 256$ using sigma notation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we must express the given series in the form

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{N}a_1 r^{n-1},
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term of the series, $r$ is the common ratio, and $N$ is the number of terms in the series. In this case, $a_1 = 1$ and $N = 5.$

To find $r,$ we calculate the ratio of the first two terms in the series:

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{-4}{1} = -4
$$

So, expressing the geometric series given in sigma notation, we obtain

$$
1 - 4 + 16 - 64 + 256 = \sum_{n=1}^{5} 1 \cdot (-4)^{n - 1}.
$$

Finally, we can simplify the above using the laws of exponents, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-4+16-64+256 & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}1\cdot (-4)^{n-1} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}(-4)^{n}(-4)^{-1} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}(-4)^{n}(-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}(-\frac{1}{4})(-4)^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Writing a Geometric Series Using Sigma Notation by Calculating the Number of Terms
canonical_examples.problem: Express the geometric series $1+ 3+ 9+ \cdots + 243$ using sigma notation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We must express the given series in the form

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{N}a_1 r^{n-1},
$$

where $a_1$ denotes the first term of the series, $r$ denotes the common ratio, and $N$ denotes the number of terms in the series. In this case, $a_1 = 1.$

To find $r,$ we find the ratio of the consecutive terms $a_1$ and $a_2 \mathbin{:}$

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{3}{1} = 3
$$

Now we must determine $N$ (the index of the last term). To do this, we use the fact that

$$
a_N  = a_1 \cdot r^{N - 1} .
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{N} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{N-1} \\ 243 & =1\cdot {3}^{N-1} \\ {3}^{5} & ={3}^{N-1} \\ 5 & =N-1 \\ N & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing the geometric series in sigma notation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}1+3+9+⋯+243 & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{6}1\cdot {3}^{n-1} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{6}{3}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Performing a Change of Variables
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the region $D$ in the $xy$-plane, given by

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq 4x+2y \leq 2, \:\: 0 \leq y-x \leq 3 \big\}.
$$

By performing the change of variables $u = 4x+2y$ and $v=y - x,$ write the following integral in terms of $u$ and $v.$ 

$$
\displaystyle 
\iint\limits_D \sin \left(3(x+y)\right)  \: \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096119/assets/b83369a26291155dbb8a5031d91fcf869cff259b7c170b6a15d58d317cee934d.png)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \, \mathrm d x \, \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v))  \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \mathrm d u \, \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u = 4x + 2y, \qquad v = y - x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096119/assets/461f793c9e8d6c3e5e5f67f846bade4acea9d40dc6c3975659d60167c33f6579.png)

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 3}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{6}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables.

In this case, we first need to solve the transformation equations

$$
u = 4x+2y, \qquad v = y-x
$$

 
for $x$ and $y$, which gives

$$
x = \dfrac{u-2v}6, \qquad y =\dfrac{u+4v}6.
$$

 

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(x+y))\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(\frac{u-2v}{6}+\frac{u+4v}{6}))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(\frac{2u+2v}{6}))|\frac{1}{6}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{2}sin\,(u+v)\,du\,dv.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Cases When the Transformation Is Inferred From the Domain
canonical_examples.problem:
Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
\displaystyle
\iint\limits_D \dfrac{y-x}{x+y} \: \mathrm{d}x \mathrm{d}y,
$$

where $D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq y-x \leq 1, \: 1 \leq x+y \leq 4 \right\}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096119/assets/039187200f0587407c67e8663de037df0a9e71155e91c4ea497e9d10d66d9119.png)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) \:  \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0 \leq y-x \leq 1, \qquad 1 \leq x+y \leq 4,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u = y-x \quad \text{and} \quad v = x+y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096119/assets/e7adae8ec845db2e091e9813a338b05895ebca800371df4841d327739863b863.png)

**Step 2**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,1\le v\le 4}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & \text{ }\text{ }1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = -\dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral.

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{y-x}{x+y}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\,|-\frac{1}{2}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{u}{v}\,du]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{v}[{\int }_{0}^{1}u\,du]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{v}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{v}\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|v|\,{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Cases When the Transformation Is Inferred From the Integrand
canonical_examples.problem:
Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
\displaystyle
\iint\limits_D (2x+y)y^2 \:\mathrm{d}x \mathrm{d}y,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $\left(\dfrac32,0\right) ,$ $\left(\dfrac52,0\right) ,$ $(1,3),$ and $(0,3).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096119/assets/039187200f0587407c67e8663de037df0a9e71155e91c4ea497e9d10d66d9119.png)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

$$

$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y) =  (2x+y)y^2
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=2x+y,
\qquad
v=y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096119/assets/88c92ebc206481c3ef86661ee413358bb060cb85f642148c609de0bf1a9da2d1.png)

**Step 2**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(\frac{3}{2},0) & =(2\cdot \frac{3}{2}+0,0) \\  & =(3,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(\frac{5}{2},0) & =(2\cdot \frac{5}{2}+0,0) \\  & =(5,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,3) & =(2\cdot 1+3,3) \\  & =(5,3) \\ {T}^{-1}(0,3) & =(2\cdot 0+3,3) \\  & =(3,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 3 \leq u \leq 5, \quad 0 \leq v \leq 3 \big\}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096119/assets/c296b1ee0451686608ec4b06c29d114ff1918233886d8471d3b2c118851aa25e.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} =\dfrac12
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral.

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y){y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{3}^{5}u{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{3}^{5}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{0}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{3}^{5}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9\cdot 8 \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating Functions Containing the Natural Logarithm
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle{\int \dfrac{3}{x \sqrt{\ln x}} \, \textrm{d}x }.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's set $u = \ln x.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac 1 x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}u=\dfrac 1 x\,{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{x\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}\,\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}\cdot \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot 2{u}^{1/2}+C \\  & =6\sqrt{u}+C \\  & =6\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating Functions Containing Other Logarithms
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate the integral $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{\log^2_3 x }{x} \,\textrm d x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \dfrac{(\log_3 x)^2 }{x} \,\textrm d x.
$$

Let $u=\log_3 x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{1}{x\ln 3}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\ln 3\,\textrm d u = \dfrac 1 x \textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3\int {u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3\cdot \frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡3({log}_{3}⁡x)^{3}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡3{log}_{3}^{3}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating Definite Integrals
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle{\int_{e}^{e^2} \dfrac{\ln^2 x}{x}\,\textrm{d}x}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's set $u = \ln x.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac 1 x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}u=\dfrac 1 x\,{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives the following:

| $x$ | $e$ | $e^2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

We now substitute and evaluate as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
	\int_{e}^{e^2} \dfrac{\ln^2 x}{x}\,\textrm{d}x
&= \int_{e}^{e^2} (\ln x)^2\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{x}\[5pt]
&=\int_{1}^{2} u^2\,\textrm{d}u\[5pt]
&=\left.\dfrac13u^{3}\right|_{1}^{2}\[5pt] 
&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(2^3-1^3 \right)\[5pt]
&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(8-1 \right)\[5pt]
&=\dfrac{7}{3}		

	}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Complement of a Union
canonical_examples.problem: If $\overline{X} = \{ a, c, d\}$ and $\overline{Y} = \{ a, e, i, o, u \},$ then what is $\overline{ X \cup Y }?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for unions states that

$$
\overline{X \cup Y} \equiv \overline{X} \cap \overline{Y}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X\cup Y} & =\overset{―}{X}\cap \overset{―}{Y} \\  & ={a,c,d}\cap {a,e,i,o,u} \\  & ={a}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Complement of an Intersection
canonical_examples.problem: If $\overline{P} = \{ 2, 4, 6 \}$ and $\overline{Q} = \{ 1, 2, 4 \},$ then what is $\overline{ P \cap Q }?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for intersections states that

$$
\overline{P \cap Q} \equiv \overline{P} \cup \overline{Q}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{P\cap Q} & =\overset{―}{P}\cup \overset{―}{Q} \\  & ={2,4,6}\cup {1,2,4} \\  & ={1,2,4,6}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Translating Contextual Problems Into Differential Equations
canonical_examples.problem: Since the year $2000$, a herd of antelopes multiplies at a rate proportional to their population. Also, the number of antelopes in the herd decreases by $20$ antelopes per year due to predators. What differential equation describes the rate of change in the population of antelopes at time $t,$ where $t$ is the time (in years) since the year $2000?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The rate of change in the number of antelopes per year increases in proportion to $P$ and decreases by $20.$ The differential equation that describes this is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}P}{\textrm{d}t}=kP - 20,
$$

where $k$ is a (positive) constant of proportionality.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Translating Coordinate Plane Problems Into Differential Equations
canonical_examples.problem: At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the derivative $y'(x)$ is **inversely** proportional to the square of the distance from $P$ to the origin. The derivative at the point $(-1,2)$ equals $2.$ What differential equation describes this curve?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the **derivative** $y'(x)$ is **inversely proportional** to the **square of the distance from $P$ to the origin.** *

We note the following:

- The *square of the distance from $P$ to the origin* is given by $x^2+y^2.$

- Since the *derivative* is *inversely proportional to* the square of the distance from $P$ to the origin, we have 

$$
y'(x) = k\cdot \dfrac{1}{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $k$ is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

$$
y'(x) = \dfrac{k}{x^2+y^2}.
$$

In addition, we're told that $y'(x) = 2$ when at the point $(-1, 2).$ We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient $k\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\frac{k}{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\ 2 & =\frac{k}{5} \\ k & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is

$$
y'(x)= \dfrac{10}{x^2+y^2}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing Two-Dimensional Related Rates Using Differential Equations
canonical_examples.problem: The area of a circle decreases at a rate that's proportional to its radius. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the radius, $r(t),$ in this process.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **area** of a circle **decreases** at a **rate** that's **proportional** to its **radius**. *

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *area $A$ of a circle* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}.
$$

- We're told that $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}$ *decreases* at a rate that's *proportional* to its *radius.* In other words,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = -kr
$$

where $k > 0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d t}.$

The area of a circle is given by 

$$
A=\pi r^2.
$$

 

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2\pi r\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-kr \\ 2\pi r\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-kr \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{kr}{2\pi r} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K = \dfrac{k}{2\pi} > 0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}t} = -K.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing Three-Dimensional Related Rates Using Differential Equations
canonical_examples.problem: The volume of a sphere increases at a rate inversely proportional to its radius. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the radius, $r(t),$ in this process.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **volume** of a sphere **increases** at a rate **inversely proportional** to its **radius**.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a sphere* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm d t}.
$$

- We're told that $\dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm d t}$ *increases* at a rate *inversely proportional to its radius.* Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm d t} = \dfrac{k}{r},
$$

where $k > 0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d t}.$

The volume $V$ of a sphere is given by

$$
V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{r} \\ 4\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{r} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{(\frac{k}{r})}{4\pi {r}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{4\pi {r}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K = \dfrac{k}{4\pi} > 0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{K}{r^3}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Sum of a Geometric Series Given in Sigma Notation
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the series $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{8} 3 (2)^{n-1}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since the given series is in the form $\displaystyle{\sum_{n=1}^N a_1 r^{n-1}},$ it is a geometric series. 

To determine the sum, we use the formula for the sum $S_N$ of a geometric series:

$$
S_N = a_1\dfrac{(1-r^N)}{1-r}
$$

In this case, $a_1 = 3,$ $r = 2,$ and $N = 8.$ If we substitute these values into the formula for $S_N,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{8}3(2)^{n-1} & =3\cdot (\frac{1-{2}^{8}}{1-2}) \\  & =3\cdot (\frac{-255}{-1}) \\  & =765\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Sum of a Simplified Geometric Series Given in Sigma Notation
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the geometric series $\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{5} 3 (4)^{n}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since the given series is in the form $\displaystyle{\sum_{n=1}^N a r^{n}},$ it is a geometric series. 

To determine the sum, we use the formula for the sum $S_N$ of a geometric series:

$$
S_N = a_1\dfrac{(1-r^N)}{1-r}
$$

In this case, $r = 4$ and $N = 5.$ We need to figure out the value of $a_1.$

The formula for the $n$th term of the series is

$$
a_n = 3(4)^n,
$$

and therefore we can calculate the first term $a_1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =3(4)^{1} \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

If we substitute $a_1 = 12,$ $r = 4,$ and $N = 5$ into the formula for $S_N,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{5}3(4)^{n} & =12\cdot \frac{(1-{4}^{5})}{1-4} \\  & =-\frac{12}{3}(-1\,023) \\  & =4\,092\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Sum of a Geometric Series by Determining the Common Ratio
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the geometric series $\displaystyle \sum_{n = 1}^{5} \dfrac{8}{2^{n-1}}\,.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that we can rewrite the series as follows:

$$
\sum_{n = 1}^{5} \dfrac{8}{2^{n-1}} = \sum_{n = 1}^{5} 8 \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^{n-1}
$$

Since the above series is in the form $\displaystyle{\sum_{n=1}^N a_1 r^{n-1}},$ it is a geometric series. 

To determine the sum, we use the formula for the sum $S_N$ of a geometric series:

$$
S_N = a_1\dfrac{(1-r^N)}{1-r}
$$

In this case, $a_1 =8,$ $r = \dfrac{1}{2},$ and $N = 5.$ If we substitute these values into the above formula, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{5}\frac{8}{{2}^{n-1}} & =8\cdot \frac{[1-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{5}]}{(1-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =8\cdot \frac{(\frac{31}{32})}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =8\cdot \frac{31}{16} \\  & =\frac{31}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Sum of a Geometric Series Given With a Zero Starting Index
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the geometric series $\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^{4} 3\left(2\right)^{n-1} .$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since the given series is in the form $\displaystyle\sum{a_1 r^{n-1}},$ it is a geometric series. Notice that the index starts from $n=0$ instead of $n=1.$

To determine the sum, we use the formula for the sum $S_N$ of a geometric series:

$$
S_N = a_0\dfrac{(1-r^N)}{1-r}
$$

Note that we use $a_0$ in the sum formula because $a_0$ is the first term of the series.

In this case, $r =2.$ Also, note that $N=5,$ since there are $5$ terms in total: $a_0,$ $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3,$ $a_4.$

The formula for the $n$th term of the series is

$$
a_n = 3\left( 2\right)^{n-1},
$$

so the first term $a_0$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =3{(2)}^{0-1} \\  & =3{(2)}^{-1} \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we substitute $a_0 =\dfrac{3}{2},$ $r=2,$ and $N=5$ into the formula for $S_N,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{5} & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{(1-{2}^{5})}{(1-2)} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{(-31)}{(-1)} \\  & =\frac{93}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Describe the set of points shown above using set-builder notation.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Linear Boundaries, One Condition
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14096165/assets/787b62fbe367feae9e4c8ed10b983a256840e3a93727fea7c1ff67cacad0129d.png)

Describe the shaded region shown above using set-builder notation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since all points $P(x,y)$ in our set lie at integer values of $x$ and $y,$ we have $x\in \mathbb Z, y\in\mathbb Z,$ and therefore 

$$
(x,y)\in \mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z = \mathbb Z^2.
$$

The points in our set include all those that lie *below* the line $y=x+2.$ For those points, the following condition is satisfied:

$$
y \lt x+2
$$

Also, notice that some points in our set lie *on* the line. We include these points by changing the inequality symbol above as follows:

$$
y \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq }x+2
$$

Therefore, we can write the set as follows:

$$
\Big\{(x,y) \in \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\mathbb Z ^2} \: : \: y \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq }x+2 \Big\}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Linear Boundaries, Two Conditions
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14096165/assets/45260087c5196cc239f21402d73169f60139bd7d2c10ee0aa1db4e1a2c56be4a.png)

Describe the shaded region shown above using set-builder notation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The points in our set include all those that lie *above* the line $y=2x$ and *below* the line $y=3.$

A point $P(x,y)$ lies *inside* the shaded region if the following conditions are satisfied:

$$
y \gt 2x, \qquad y < 3.
$$

Combining this into a single condition, we have

$$
2x \lt y < 3.
$$

We must also include the line $y= 3$ since the boundary is included in the set (the curve is solid). So, we change the corresponding inequality symbol above as follows:

$$
2x \lt y  \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq } 3
$$

Moreover, since we're considering *every* real value in this region, $x\in \mathbb R, y\in\mathbb R,$ and therefore 

$$
(x,y)\in \mathbb R\times\mathbb R = \mathbb R^2.
$$

Therefore, we can write the set as

$$
\Big\{(x,y)\in \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\mathbb R^2 } \: : \:  2x \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\lt } y \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq } 3 \Big\}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Describing Non-Rectangular Sets Using Set-Builder Notation
canonical_examples.problem:
Use set builder notation to describe the shaded region given in the diagram below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14096165/assets/e5f5f2f2e67ba0ad566b2759ca5536d248f671bf0f082d567a7f7d993772601e.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1.
$$

 

Here, the elliptical boundary of our region has horizontal radius $a=5$ and vertical radius $b=4.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which we can write as

$$
16x^2 + 25y^2 = 400.
$$

We're interested in describing all points that lie *outside* the ellipse. So, let's pick any point outside the region, say, $(10,0).$ Substituting its coordinates into the equation of the boundary, we obtain

$$
16(10)^2+25(0)^2 \: {\color{blue}>} \: 400.
$$

As a result, the points $P(x,y)$ in our region are any real numbers that satisfy the condition

$$
16x^2 + 25y^2  \gt 400.
$$

We must also include the curve $16x^2 + 25y^2 = 400$ since the boundary is included in the set (the curve is solid). So, we change the inequality symbol above as follows:

$$
16x^2 + 25y^2  \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\geq } 400.
$$

Therefore, we can write the set as

$$
\Big\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \: : \: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}16 }x^2 + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}25 }y^2  \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\geq } 400 \bigg\}.
$$
